doc.title: Håkan Rydin interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016

title: Jazz as international; wanting to sound American, now proud to sound Swedish
summary: Rydin talks about jazz's global spread and how he moved from wanting an American sound to embracing a Scandinavian one.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well we’re in Glasgow and you’re from Sweden and I’m from America, and it says something about jazz. How’s your feeling about coming to a place like this and playing for an international audience?

Well, as you say, jazz is truly international, and maybe more now than ever before. I think now it is not as clear a jazz center in the world like it used to be in New York City and 42nd Street and all that stuff. I mean now, in all of the world, in every town or city of some size you have a jazz club, you have jazz education, and you have enormous festivals. And you have good musicians all over the world. So it’s truly international.
Did you ever have aspirations like some European musicians to relocate to New York City?

Well maybe when I was very young. But not really, not really. When I was, as I say, 18, 20, of course I did want to sound like an American musician. We all were. And I remember the first time we went to Canada, to festivals there, at a pretty young age, in the reviews, it said, “typical Scandinavian sound” or “European sound.” And we were so sorry about that because we wanted to sound American. But things have changed. I’m 65
now and I’m proud to sound Scandinavian. I’m proud to sound Swedish. And I try to do it, in a way, even if it’s international. But I play some Swedish folk music as well.
